headline: Here the same character is read twice, once the native way and once the Chinese way.
Monday is “moon day”, a name that came from Chinese astrology in the Heian period.
Tuesday is “Mars day”, a name that came from Chinese astrology in the Heian period.
Wednesday is “Mercury day”, a name that came from Chinese astrology in the Heian period.
Thursday is “Jupiter day”, a name that came from Chinese astrology in the Heian period.
Friday is “Venus day”, a name that came from Chinese astrology in the Heian period.
Saturday is “Saturn day”, and its 日 voices to び.
Sunday is “Sun day”, and the -day compound first appears in 1826.
A well is a “water-well place” — and the 戸 in it may not be a door at all.
To swear an oath may once have meant to “mix blood”.
A blackboard is a “black board” — and a native reading says the same with kuro and ita.
Twins are a “set of two” “children”, with こ voiced to ご.
Gas is an English word — but it also has a kanji spelling picked only for the sound.
A son is a “begotten child” — and the 息 is a borrowed stand-in.
“Cute” began as “embarrassing, shameful” — and the kanji have nothing to do with the sound.
Rōmaji has no “n” in it — the Roman part is Portuguese-derived ローマ with the Chinese-derived “character” 字.
The thumb is the “parent finger”.
Okurigana are the kana “sent along afterward” — and the word is first attested in 1477.
Oxygen is “sour element” — a calque of Dutch from the same 1834 book as hydrogen.
A cavity is a “bug tooth”, with は voiced to ば.
The “wasei-eigo” motorcycle is, Wiktionary says, actually a real English word.
A baby is “red” plus an affectionate suffix, from the colour of a newborn's skin.
“Three days” grew out of an earlier “mika”, with a tensed sound added.
The toilet is the “place of convenience” — a coinage that Wiktionary dates to the late 1400s.
Kana means “borrowed name” — characters lent for their sounds.
A bar is a “drink place”, using an older form of the word for sake.
A study is a “reading room”, first attested in the late 800s.
To repeat is to “reel” and “return”.
The piano is a clipped “pianoforte” — or a plain Italian word, depending on the source.
“News” ends in ス, not ズ — an English /z/ heard as an s.
A single month, ひとつき, may be an old “one month” — and Chinese-derived readings of the same spelling sit alongside it.
